Therefore, the two phonological measures were entered together in hierarchical multiple regression analyses (HMR), and their importance relative to each VAS test was assessed separately for WordID and spelling. The results for PreProbe are shown in Table 3 and those for PosProbe in Table 4. Because age was correlated with PosProbe, it was included in the PosProbe analyses. As shown in the tables, the unique contributions of the phonological measures to literacy were substantial while those of the VAS tests were comparatively trivial.

Below Tables 3 and 4 are reported the contributions when PWPron is excluded from analyses.

Table 5 shows the individual coefficients for the analyses in the two tables. While PWPron (coding) was a strong unique predictor of literacy, especially spelling, Spoonerisms (sensitivity) was significant only for reading. 45 PWPron to spelling than reading, together with a slightly larger correlation of PosProbe than PreProbe with Spoonerisms. The latter result may reflect the working memory demands of PosProbe and Spoonerisms. Importantly, overall, the two VAS tests (unexpectedly) showed similar associations with the DVs and the traditional predictors of literacy skills.

Implications of adult data for reading development

The correlations of the VAS tests with literacy were considerably lower than is typical in developmental studies. It is possible that VAS is a causal factor in reading acquisition, but in well-practised adult readers it may not substantially limit reading performance. Against this argument, phonological sensitivity plays no direct role in accomplished reading, yet the present adult sample showed a substantial correlation between literacy and the Spoonerism test of phonological sensitivity. It appears that cognitive skills that are important for literacy acquisition continue to be associated with adult literacy (Castles et al., 2018; Pennington et al., 1987; Perfetti, 2007). Likewise, if VAS indexes a causal variable that supports word identification, then it can be expected to support word identification in adults. Consequently there is good reason to suppose that the present results with adults have implications for literacy development.

Traditional predictors of literacy

Results involving the traditional predictors were largely as expected. Our observed correlation of r = .55 between WordID and spelling is typical for adults (Cunningham & Stanovich, 1990; Stanovich et al., 1991). The similarity of results for WordID and spelling fits the consensus that phonological skills support the acquisition of high-quality orthographic and phonological representations of words, and that these representations serve both reading and spelling (Burt & Tate, 2002; Holmes & Ng, 1993). The phonological skills PWPron (coding) and Spoonerisms (sensitivity) were correlated with each other (cf. Treiman & Baron, 1983) and as expected, both, especially PWPron, predicted each of the two DVs.

The ART is somewhat insensitive, and the mean corrected for false alarms was low.

Nonetheless, the present ART correlated moderately-to-strongly with WordID and spelling.

The correlation of the ART with PWPron, though larger than expected, aligns with evidence that reading experience impacts spelling-sound knowledge (Vellutino, 1994). Individuals with good phonological skills may also find reading easier and thus read more than others. This possibility may also explain the unexpected correlation of Spoonerisms with the ART.

Role of VAS in reading vs. spelling

As Ans et al. (1998) noted in their computational model that was the impetus for the VAS test, a global strategy for processing letter strings is employed for reading familiar words, whereas unfamiliar words and nonwords are largely read by an analytic strategy that segments letter strings. Van den Boer et al. (2015) observed that the association between phonological coding (PWPron) and VAS that is commonly reported cannot be based on the role of VAS as a measure of the global strategy, given that this strategy is not available for unfamiliar items. The effectiveness of the global strategy (and hence VAS) is potentially relevant only to reading already-learned words, and thus is difficult to disentangle from reading experience. Spelling is more heavily dependent on the quality of orthographic representations than is reading, with some effective readers being poor spellers (Andrews et al., 2020). Establishing new orthographic representations for unfamiliar words must rely on the analytic strategy, and it is uncertain to what extent the global strategy supports the updating of orthographic representations. Arguably, support for the VAS hypothesis would be stronger if VAS accuracy were more closely correlated with word reading than with pseudoword pronunciation or spelling.

Relations of VAS with phonology

Our evidence suggests that VAS-literacy associations are not independent of phonological skills. Our VAS tests had similar associations with PWPron (coding) and Spoonerisms (sensitivity), perhaps reflecting the high demands of Spoonerisms, as well as the presumed causal role of sensitivity in the acquisition of coding skills. As noted, phonological sensitivity often has non-significant correlations with VAS.

Phonological coding supports short term serial recall of verbal material (Baddeley & Hitch, 1994), and dyslexia is associated with deficits in this task (Rapala & Brady, 1990).

Consequently we expected that phonological coding would no longer predict VAS accuracy when the working memory demand was substantially reduced. This expectation was disconfirmed; the PreProbe VAS test designed to have a low memory load, like the PosProbe test, showed small but significant correlations with literacy. As indicated in the Results section, there are several sources of evidence that the memory load was successfully reduced for the PreProbe test. We conclude that the VAS-literacy association may indeed depend on phonological coding but not necessarily on verbal working memory. We discuss two possibilities below; namely, a direct effect of phonological coding on speeded letter identification, and an effect that arises in the context of a reverse causation account of the VAS-literacy association. These possibilities cannot be evaluated as causes in the present cross-sectional correlational data, but potentially inform future research on VAS and its importance.

Possibility 1: Does phonological coding affect letter identification under time pressure?

In addition to its role in literacy, phonological coding may support letter identification and decision making in VAS tasks. The correlations between phonological sensitivity and VAS equally fit with this account given that phonological sensitivity is thought to play a causal role in phonological coding skill.

Pre-reading children at risk of dyslexia show weaker phonological skills and slower acquisition of letter knowledge (Hindson et al., 2005), while adults with weaker phonological skills may be slow to name letters. Proficient performance under time pressure in VAS tests plausibly relies not only on fluent letter identification, but also on the efficient use of letter names (phonology) in decision-making and response preparation. As noted, in VAS tests with unnameable symbols instead of letters, mean accuracy has been low (less than 40%), except in a less demanding test in which children chose, after each trial, between the target and an item that did not appear in the sequence (Ziegler et al., 2010). Low accuracy with symbols suggests an important role for item naming in VAS performance. In our study, weaker phonological coding in some participants may have slowed letter name activation and, especially under time pressure, made their phonological representations noisier and more vulnerable to mutual interference. In summary, phonological skills may support speeded letter identification in VAS and literacy, explaining the association between the latter two constructs.

We sought to test this explanation in an exploratory analysis. A signature effect of the deployment of phonological coding in short-term serial recall tasks is the phonological similarity effect, namely, poorer ordered short-term recall when all list items are phonologically similar than when they are dissimilar (Baddeley & Hitch, 1994). However, phonological similarity of some items typically enhances (unordered) memory for these items (Nairne & Kelley, 2004; Smith & Jarrold, 2014).

We categorised letters as phonologically similar or not, based on the memory confusion data of Conrad (1964), and analysed PosProbe and probe-present (yes) PreProbe trials. In the latter task, we assessed the effect of similarity of the probe to another letter in the sequence. The VAS hypothesis would be most favoured if phonological similarity was unrelated to performance. However, in both VAS tasks, trials on which the probe/target letter was phonologically similar to one other sequence letter (SIM) had higher accuracy and faster latencies (for correct responses) than trials with no similar sequence letter (DISS). For PosProbe the mean accuracy was .75 for SIM and .7 for DISS , F(1, 262) = 46.9, p < .001, ηp² = .15, and the mean latencies were 1028 ms and 1047 ms respectively, F(1, 261) = 65.25, p =.023, ηp² = .02. For PreProbe trials on which the probe was present, accuracy was higher on SIM trials (M = .89) than DISS trials (M = .75), F(1, 262) = 199.00, p < .001, ηp² = .43, and response latencies were shorter for SIM trials (645 ms) than on DISS trials (673 ms), F(1, 255) = 5.22, p = .023, ηp² = .02.

In summary, the results indicate that phonological similarity between a target and another sequence item facilitates letter naming and thus task accuracy in both VAS tasks. In turn, this result weakens the view that VAS is a predictor or cause of literacy skills that is independent of phonological skills.

Possibility 2: VAS, reading, and reverse causation?

Another possible explanation for the associations between VAS and phonological skills is that reverse causation is at work: Reading skill and experience affect letter identification efficiency and VAS. If this account is correct, the fact that phonological skills have a causal role in reading acquisition means that they in turn are likely to be associated with VAS. There was only modest support for reverse causation in our results, with a small correlation (r = .13) between PreProbe and the ART measure of reading experience, and a trend (p = .069) for a correlation between PosProbe and the ART when age was controlled.

The correlation with the ART may be small because most university students and other highly literate adults have had sufficient reading practice to have reached a plateau on visual letter processing. Therefore, many below-average scorers on the ART may have had sufficient reading experience to perform well on the VAS tests. Consequently, the reverse causation hypothesis remains viable although the ART did not produce compelling evidence for it.

Conclusions

In line with a large body of evidence (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012), the traditional predictors of literacy skills, namely phonological skills and reading experience, had moderate or strong relationships with literacy measures. Meanwhile, the smaller VAS-literacy correlations in our adult sample, and in developmental studies controlling for age (and thus in part for reading experience and memory skills), work against the causal importance of VAS in reading development (Bosse et al., 2007; Saksida et al., 2016; Zoubrinetzky et al., 2016).

Additionally, after controlling phonological ability, the present VAS measures only weakly predicted literacy, with the PosProbe-spelling association becoming non-significant. Thus, there was little support for VAS as an independent causal factor in reading acquisition.

The present cross-sectional correlational study cannot allow causal inferences to be drawn, but does suggest possible explanations for the small associations we observed between VAS and literacy measures. Specifically, these associations might be explained as a) effects of phonological skills on speeded letter identification in VAS and on literacy or b) results of reading experience and skill. In any case, the present results show, in line with the conclusions of Saksida et al. (Saksida et al., 2016), that any causal role of visual attention span in literacy acquisition is substantially less important than the role of phonological skills.

Discussion

The aim of the present study with adults was to assess a new low-memory version of the VAS test (of letters) against a traditional partial report VAS test in its associations with literacy. The study was novel in that both word reading and spelling were dependent measures, and a measure of print exposure was included to provide information on possible effects of reading experience on VAS. Also novel in adult studies, the traditional predictors phonological skills and print exposure provided a benchmark against which to assess the prediction by VAS.

As expected, the two DVs WordID and spelling were strongly correlated. The results for the VAS tests did not fully align with predictions or with prior findings by Valdois and colleagues (Bosse et al., 2007). Both the partial report PosProbe test and the low-memory PreProbe test correlated weakly-to-moderately (r = .23 to .30) with WordID and spelling.

There was evidence that VAS is not independent of phonological abilities, given that the VAS tests also correlated weakly-to-moderately (r = .22 to .28) with both phonological coding (PWPron) and sensitivity (Spoonerisms). Furthermore, phonological skills accounted for substantial variance in literacy unaccounted for by VAS, as expected, while VAS accounted for little unique variance. Little change in the unique contribution of VAS was observed when PWPron was dropped from the phonological measures.

The pattern of associations suggests some conclusions about the nature of the connection between VAS tests and literacy. Of course, no conclusions about causation can be drawn in the present cross-sectional correlational study.

The two VAS tests compared

The regression analyses indicate that the traditional PosProbe test had a slightly stronger unique association with word identification than PreProbe, but both associations were significant. By contrast, for spelling, PreProbe made a small but significant unique prediction whereas PosProbe did not.

The remaining 264 (Mage = 22.5 years, range 17 to 62, SD = 8.34) were Introductory Psychology students receiving course credit (N = 137) and community volunteers (N = 127). A program error precluded gender data for 25 participants, with missing values recorded for analyses; 65% of the remainder were women. The University of Queensland Human Research Ethics Committee approved the study as compliant with the guidelines of the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (no. 2023/HE000127). All participants gave informed consent and received feedback on the aims of the study. The data were anonymous.
